_meta.title: Recommendation pilot — everyday AI assistants
_meta.purpose: Test whether ValueCompass can support one useful recommendation journey. Deliberately narrow: one category, six alternatives, four criteria. Not a general scoring layer.
_meta.provenance_note: Every finding here was produced by a model reading a source, not by a human re-reading it. Nothing is marked human-reviewed. Where a fetch failed or a source did not carry the claim, that is recorded rather than filled in.

claim_types.established_outcome: A thing that happened or a state recorded in a filing, licence, index or court record.
claim_types.company_statement: The company's own description of itself. True as a statement; the underlying fact may be unverified.
claim_types.commitment: A stated future intention. Check whether it is binding, and whether it has since been withdrawn.
claim_types.allegation: A claim made by a party to a dispute, not settled.
claim_types.third_party_report: An outlet's characterisation. Check whether it cites a filing or is inference.

rules.unknown: Unknown is neither a positive nor a negative finding. It never counts toward or against an alternative.
rules.hard_requirement: An unknown hard requirement remains unconfirmed. The alternative is not shortlisted and is not excluded — it is unassessable.
rules.shortlist: A shortlist is produced only where the evidence supports one. Slots are never filled to reach a target number.

category.label: Everyday AI assistants
category.definition: A general-purpose conversational assistant a non-specialist uses for drafting, summarising, explaining and answering questions, through a chat interface.

why_this_category.user_relevance: It is the highest-frequency, most personal AI choice most people make, it is genuinely substitutable — switching costs are a habit and a subscription, not a data migration — and the same task can be done by any of the alternatives, so the choice really can turn on values rather than capability.
why_this_category.evidence_coverage: Six of the providers are already makers in this dataset, so no new entity set is needed. It is also the category where the strongest surviving evidence sits: model access and licensing is publicly checkable from licence files, and provider governance is covered by proxy statements and charters. Categories like AI coding tools would have failed on both counts — thinner governance records and much weaker substitutability.
why_this_category.honest_caveat: Capability differences between these products are real and are not assessed here. This pilot answers 'which of these fits what I care about', not 'which is best at the task'.

functional_requirements.label: General-purpose conversational assistant
functional_requirements.why: Without this the alternatives are not substitutes.

functional_requirements.label: Usable by an individual without a developer account
functional_requirements.why: The journey is a consumer choice, not an API integration.

functional_requirements.label: Some no-cost entry path
functional_requirements.why: Not required by every user, but it changes who can act on a recommendation.

criteria.label: Voting control
criteria.concept: Whether an individual or small group can outvote everyone else on governance. Distinct from owning the upside.
criteria.why_users_care: It determines who can reverse a commitment. A company can be widely owned and still be controlled by two people.

criteria.label: Economic ownership concentration
criteria.concept: Who holds the financial upside, and how concentrated it is. Distinct from who can vote.
criteria.why_users_care: It shows who is enriched by the product's success, which is a different question from who directs it.

criteria.label: Public-benefit commitment structure
criteria.concept: Whether a legal structure obliges the company to weigh non-shareholder interests — and whether it is binding, revocable, or a pledge.
criteria.why_users_care: It is the difference between a stated intention and one someone can enforce.
criteria.note: A commitment that was later withdrawn is evidence about the company, not a neutral absence.

criteria.label: Model access and licensing
criteria.concept: Whether the model weights are published, under what licence, and whether a user could run them independently of the provider.
criteria.why_users_care: It is the practical measure of whether leaving is possible. It is also the criterion this dataset can currently evidence best — licences are public, versioned and checkable.
criteria.selection_note: Chosen partly because it is well-evidenced. That is a stated bias and it favours the open-weight providers. It was not chosen because it produces a convenient winner — it produces an uncomfortable one, since the best-evidenced option on this criterion is also the one whose consumer product we could not confirm exists.

findings.claim: Larry Page and Sergey Brin together control 52.7% of Alphabet's total voting power. Class B shares carry ten votes each and are held by insiders; Class C carries none.
findings.source: Alphabet 2026 annual meeting proxy statement, via search of proxy reporting
findings.scope: Alphabet Inc., the parent. Does not separately describe governance of the Google DeepMind subsidiary.
findings.uncertainty: The percentage was read from reporting of the proxy, not from the filing document itself. The figure is specific and internally consistent (Page 27.1% + Brin 25.2% = 52.3%, reported total 52.7%), but a direct read of the filing would settle it.

findings.claim: Anthropic is a Delaware Public Benefit Corporation. A Long-Term Benefit Trust holds Class T shares carrying no economic rights, which elect an increasing number of a seven-member board, intended to reach a majority.
findings.source: Anthropic's own description of the Trust, as reported 2026-08-19
findings.scope: Corporate governance of Anthropic. Says nothing about the Claude product.
findings.uncertainty: The reporting outlet characterises the board-election mechanism rather than quoting a charter, and notes the IPO prospectus was confidential at the time of writing.

findings.claim: Founders are reported to be receiving a new class of stock with enhanced voting rights ahead of the IPO. The vote ratio has not been disclosed and Anthropic has not commented on specifics.
findings.uncertainty: High. The central number — the vote ratio — is explicitly undisclosed. This is the kind of claim that cannot drive a decision either way.

findings.claim: The Long-Term Benefit Trust had three trustees as of 2026-08-19, reduced from four after a trustee departed on 2026-08-04.
findings.scope: Trust composition on that date only. A trust's membership changes; this is a snapshot.
findings.uncertainty: The 2023 description of the Trust said five members. The reduction to three is recent and the direction of travel is unclear.

findings.claim: OpenAI operates as a for-profit PBC controlled by the nonprofit OpenAI Foundation. The capped-profit mechanism was removed in the October 2025 recapitalisation.
findings.source: Contemporaneous reporting cited in makers.json; OpenAI's own structure page was not reachable in this pass (HTTP 403).
findings.scope: Corporate structure as at the recapitalisation.
findings.uncertainty: Carried forward from the existing dataset record, not re-verified against a primary source in this pass. The withdrawal of the profit cap is the decision-relevant part and is well attested.

findings.claim: After the October 2025 recapitalisation the OpenAI Foundation holds about 26% and controls the board, Microsoft about 27%, and about 47% sits with employees and investors.
findings.scope: Ownership at the recapitalisation. Eleven months old at time of research.

findings.claim: Amazon holds roughly 15–19% and Google roughly 14% of Anthropic's economics.
findings.uncertainty: Not re-verified in this pass. Predates the IPO reporting above, which implies the cap table has since changed.

findings.claim: DeepSeek-R1 weights are published under the MIT licence, downloadable from Hugging Face, and permit commercial use, modification and derivative works including distillation.
findings.source: DeepSeek-R1 repository licence file and model card
findings.scope: The R1 model weights. Not the consumer app, and not the current V4 flagship, whose licence was not checked.
findings.uncertainty: Low for R1 itself. The gap is that the user-facing product may not run R1: the hosted reasoner alias was retired 2026-07-24.

findings.claim: Mistral publishes open weights for its current lineup: Large 3 and Small 4 under Apache 2.0, Medium 3.5 under a modified MIT licence, all self-hostable with commercial use and fine-tuning permitted.
findings.source: Secondary aggregator coverage of Mistral's model documentation
findings.scope: Model weights. Le Chat the product is a hosted service built on them.
findings.uncertainty: Moderate. Mistral's own documentation was not read directly; the 'modified MIT' terms for Medium 3.5 in particular need reading before being relied on, because a modified permissive licence can carry use restrictions.

findings.claim: The model behind ChatGPT is not published as downloadable weights.
findings.uncertainty: Widely understood and consistent with the FMTI scoring of o3 as a closed model, but not checked against a source in this pass. Recorded as unverified rather than assumed.

findings.claim: The model behind Claude is not published as downloadable weights.
findings.uncertainty: Same as above — likely, unchecked, recorded as unverified.

findings.claim: Gemini flagship weights are not published, though Google publishes the separate Gemma open-weight family.
findings.source: Not verified in this pass; Gemma appears in the makers.json product record
findings.scope: Gemma is a different model family from the one behind the Gemini assistant. Treating Gemma as portability for a Gemini user would be a category error.

findings.claim: Microsoft is described in the existing dataset as a widely held public company with no founder control bloc.
findings.source: makers.json record, which carries no source for this claim
findings.uncertainty: This is exactly the kind of unsourced record the evidence rule excludes. A proxy statement would settle it in one read; none was consulted.

findings.claim: Founder Liang Wenfeng is recorded as controlling roughly 89.5% via the High-Flyer parent.
findings.source: makers.json record, which carries no source for this claim
findings.uncertainty: Unsourced in the dataset and not verified here. If true it is decisive for the voting-control criterion, which makes leaving it unverified the more serious gap.

c_voting_control.note: One of six. The single assessable alternative fails the criterion.

c_economic_ownership.note: Both assessable findings are carried from the dataset rather than re-verified, and both are dated.

c_public_benefit.note: For the other four, no public-benefit structure is recorded. That is an absence of record, not a finding that none exists.

c_model_access.note: The best-covered criterion, and the only one where a positive finding exists for more than one alternative.
